My own HTTP attack against the running demo (attack/http_attack.py, http_attack.out) signed in as alnoor admin (cookie and bearer), viewer, noaccess and anonymous. It sent 2,526 requests carrying gulfsteel ids in routes, 8 tenant-switch header variants including X-Erp-Workspace and Host, tenant query names, body tenantId/workspaceId fields, and every B e-mail, name and role name through search/q/email/code/name/filter. biggest_gap.title: The isolation gate guesses tenant-switch inputs instead of proving the tenant can only come from the session
biggest_gap.detail:
G1 HTTP sends tenant B's id in only six fixed header names (X-Tenant-Id, X-Tenant, Tenant-Id, X-Company-Id, X-Forwarded-Host, an erp_tenant cookie) and three fixed body names (tenantId, tenant_id, companyId). Body uuid fields otherwise get a random B id, so the tenant id lands there only by chance. Nothing checks how the tenant gets bound. Any code may call set_config('app.tenant_id', …) or IgnoreQueryFilters(), and nothing checks that the tenant each request's SQL runs under is the signed-in user's tenant. An endpoint that switches tenant on any header or field name not in those lists passes the whole gate, even though the spec says the tenant comes only from the session. Every later module (contacts, documents, imports, jobs) adds handlers that could do this.

Fix:
(a) A source gate, like the existing one for reviewed functions: only ErpDbSession may name app.tenant_id or app.tenant_tx, and IgnoreQueryFilters/FromSql only in reviewed files.
(b) A runtime check in the existing SqlTrace: inside an authenticated request, every statement after binding must run with current_tenant_id() equal to the principal's tenant claim.
(c) A deterministic phase that sends B's tenant id in every uuid body field and in every X-* header seen in the app's source.

A related G2 blind spot: a POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE endpoint may declare a *.read permission. A cheap rule (state-changing methods never declare an action named read) closes it.
biggest_gap.evidence: In a clone of c71d20e, apply gauntlet/evidence/p00-foundation/r2/plant-A-hdr.diff. It is about 8 lines in UserEndpoints.List: when an X-Erp-Workspace header holds a uuid, it runs SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', @t, true) on the request's connection and queries with IgnoreQueryFilters(). Run `dotnet test tests/Erp.Gates.Tests -c Release`: 45/45 pass, rc=0 (plant-A-hdr.log). Then add plant-A-hdr-proof-test.cs under tests/Erp.Gates.Tests/CriticProof/ and run it with --filter CriticProof. It passes: GET /api/identity/users?take=5 with X-Erp-Workspace: <tenant B id>, signed in as tenant A admin, returns tenant B users (viewer@bravo-cnry….example, 'Mariam Al Mansoori CNRY…' canary names; plant-A-hdr-proof.log). For G2: apply plant-P2.diff and the suite passes 45/45 (plant-P2.log). plant-P2-proof-test.cs shows a user holding only identity.users.read reactivating a deactivated user (204).

other_findings: The product's defence in depth works: with only the set_config plant (no IgnoreQueryFilters), the EF global filter still returned an empty list. The leak needs both bugs. Today no code under src/ reads a tenant from a request header or query, or calls IgnoreQueryFilters or FromSql.

Round 1 gaps stay fixed. A lookup endpoint calling resolve_login is now blocked by the unbound-only guard (0 rows inside a bound transaction), and by the source and trace gates. The round 1 create-user escalation plant (P3) is caught by 2 tests. ModuleBuilder.List exists. Plural messages are right in English and Arabic ('1 user', 'مستخدم واحد', '100,004 مستخدمين'). The libgssapi error line is gone from ./erp up.
Ratchet held. Suite 126 .NET, 19 web unit and 9 e2e meet the committed minimums, and every count rose from round 1's 97/13/8. The ratchet file was not loosened.

The sign-in lockout counter still increments on every account with the same e-mail in every tenant. Knowing a tenant B address lets anyone pause B's sign-in for 15 minutes with 5 bad passwords. This is not a data leak, but there is no per-account throttle or CAPTCHA. The Arabic and English error text also states the policy (5 attempts, 15 minutes).

The app role can call identity.resolve_login(email) on an unbound connection and get any tenant's tenant_id, user_id and password hash (db-attack-app-role.txt). This is the reviewed sign-in path, and the HTTP surface does not expose it. It does mean any SQL injection in the app reads every tenant's credential hashes.

Users search uses ILIKE '%term%' on email_normalized and display_name. There is no trigram index, only a btree on (tenant_id, display_name). Searches took 196-350 ms over 100,004 users here, which is fine now. It will not hold for p05/p16 at 100k+ rows with joins.
The Arabic screens show Latin digits (100,004; 2026/10/02). That is acceptable for the UAE, but there is no per-user numeral choice yet.

Switching language in the shell flips to RTL in 24 ms and saves to the profile (PUT /me/preferences 200, audited). If the page reloads before that request returns, the old language comes back from the session. This is minor.
Money has a value type (decimal amount, currency, rate, base amount; numeric(19,4)/(19,8)), but no table stores money yet, and the type does not carry the base currency's code.
A fresh visit logs a 401 from the session probe as a console error. It is cosmetic.
